title: Service
hookLine: a regular act of service to someone in need
tomorrow: after five years, is there anything left to learn?

cards: Schools and parishes put out the sign-up sheet: the food drive, the coat drive, the shift at the shelter. In December it fills up. By February, it can look a lot emptier.
It isn't that people stop caring. A single act is easy to sign up for; a habit needs a slot. Mercy on a calendar looks less like a big moment and more like a Saturday that repeats.

teach.b: Jesus draws the picture in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in."

Then the line that surprises everyone in the story, the sheep and the goats alike: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Neither group knew whom they'd been serving.
That's the hinge. Service isn't a favor done for Christ; it's meeting him.
The Church draws its works of mercy from this list, feeding the hungry, visiting the sick and the prisoner, so they can be scheduled, not just felt.

teach.h: THE PIECE THAT GOES OUT THE DOOR.
teach.b: And that's the point for a rule of life: one act of service that repeats. A monthly shift. A weekly visit.
A neighbor whose groceries you carry every Thursday.
The Church adds spiritual works of mercy too: comforting the sorrowful, forgiving, praying for the living and the dead. The rule now has prayer, Sunday, confession and scripture.
Service is the piece that goes out the door.

how: Catholics practice the corporal works of mercy through parish food pantries, visits to the sick and imprisoned, and groups like the St. Vincent de Paul Society, often on a regular schedule.

games.q: your friend wants to help after a flood: one huge weekend, or two hours every month at the shelter. what fits a rule of life?
o: the monthly two hours; mercy that repeats becomes part of the rule.
the huge weekend; one big act counts more than many small ones.
neither, until she can manage to do both perfectly.
games.why: both are real mercy. but for a rule of life, the one that repeats is the one that lasts.

practice: Pick one place or person who could use a regular hand: a pantry, a neighbor, a grandparent. Send one message now asking when they could use you, and put a date on it. Then rest; the asking is the first act.

wordCard.voice: Service. A regular act of mercy for someone in need, where Jesus says he is met.

orig.note: Greek: service. the New Testament word for serving, from tables (Acts 6:1) to the whole church.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: regular mercy, not a big moment but a Saturday that repeats. That's the week.
